title: Moody's: US Life Insurers' Private and Illiquid Bonds Reach $807 Billion, 20% of Fixed Income, With Concentration and PIK Risks to Watch
summary: Moody's report of June 8, 2026 says private and illiquid bonds at US life insurers reached $807 billion at end-2025, up from $685 billion, with the ten largest holding 44% and four areas flagged for monitoring.
description:
Private credit has become a core part of how US life insurers invest, and Moody's Ratings says that the shift carries risks that deserve close attention. In a report published on June 8, 2026, and covered by Insurance Business and Reinsurance News, Moody's said the industry's private and illiquid bonds reached $807 billion at year-end 2025. That is about 20% of the industry's $4 trillion fixed income portfolio, up from $685 billion, or 18%, a year earlier, an increase of $122 billion in one year. Moody's called the shift structural rather than cyclical. This article summarises the report as covered by those outlets. An earlier version relied mainly on the Barclays growth figure and the Proskauer default index; the Moody's figures themselves are now set out first.

How does Moody's define the assets? According to Reinsurance News, Moody's defines private credit as non-bank lending. For insurers this includes commercial real estate and mortgage loans and traditional private placements. Of the $807 billion, bonds carrying a private-letter rating (PL) account for $483 billion, or 12% of bonds, Z-rated bonds for $81 billion, or about 2%, and other Level 3 holdings for $242 billion, or 6%. By composition, 64% is issuer credit obligations such as corporate debt, loans, project finance and REIT and BDC obligations, while 36% is asset-backed securities. Moody's says growth is spreading into real estate debt, infrastructure debt and asset-based finance, including private ABS, fund finance and data centre securitisations. Demand is driven by higher risk-adjusted yields and by more privately originated credit opportunities. Insurers get access through direct origination platforms, partnerships with asset managers and affiliated asset management structures.

What are the four areas Moody's is watching? First, concentration. The ten largest insurers hold $352 billion, or 44%, of the private illiquid bonds, while holding only 24% of total industry fixed income. Second, a widening credit-quality gap. Reinsurance News reports that 91% of the $807 billion carries an investment-grade-equivalent designation from the NAIC's Securities Valuation Office. By NAIC category, 49% is NAIC 1, 43% is NAIC 2 and 9% is below investment grade. The wider $4 trillion portfolio is 95% investment grade, with 59% in NAIC 1, 36% in NAIC 2 and 5% below investment grade. Moody's said that impairment rates in private credit could exceed those of liquid holdings in a downside scenario. Third, structural complexity. Asset-backed securities made up 38% of 2025 purchases, against 27% of existing holdings, which Moody's described as a deliberate strategic shift rather than passive drift. Fourth, payment-in-kind (PIK) instruments, where a borrower pays interest by adding to the debt instead of paying cash. PIK exposure equals 1.1% of statutory surplus, which Moody's views as moderate and not currently a material threat to balance sheets, but a possible late-cycle warning indicator. Insurers with the highest PIK balances relative to surplus include Resolution Life US, Genworth, Security Benefit, Wilton Re and Sammons, according to Reinsurance News. Moody's also cautions that headline PIK numbers may understate exposure, because bonds issued by business development companies may not show PIK even when their underlying borrowers use it.

Where is the stress emerging? Moody's says risks are emerging mainly in middle-market direct lending, where credit quality is weakening and borrower stress is rising. It also notes that, under narrower definitions of private credit, exposure is more limited, and that most reported exposure is investment grade. Moody's expects private credit corporate lending assets to exceed $2 trillion in 2026 and approach $4 trillion by 2030.

What other data points are cited? Insurance Business cites Barclays as finding that US life insurers' private credit holdings grew by more than 20% in 2025, with exposure above 15% of investments at some private-equity-affiliated insurers, including Apollo-backed Athene and KKR-backed Global Atlantic. It also cites the Proskauer Private Credit Default Index, which tracks 697 loans totalling $189.2 billion and reported a default rate of 2.73% in the first quarter of 2026, up from 1.84% two quarters earlier. Those figures come from different sources and use different definitions, so they should not be added together or compared directly with Moody's numbers.

What are regulators doing? The article says the National Association of Insurance Commissioners' 2025 Principles-Based Bond Definition lets it challenge the classification of complex assets, and that higher defaults could lead to capital charges. NAIC president Scott White has named transparency in life insurance portfolios as a top 2026 regulatory priority. The US Treasury convened domestic and international insurance regulators earlier in 2026 to discuss private credit risks. From year-end 2025 statutory filings, insurers must give more detailed bond disclosures, separating issuer credit obligations from structured ABS. In its commentary, Moody's stressed governance, stress testing and capital planning.

What does this mean for policyholders? Life insurers and annuity providers use long-term assets to match long-term promises, and illiquid assets can be a natural fit for that. The risk Moody's points to is not that policies are about to fail, but that concentration, weaker credit quality in some segments and complexity could make the system more vulnerable in a downturn. Those with annuities or life policies can look at their insurer's financial strength rating and ask how much of its portfolio is in private and structured assets.

The wider message is that private credit is no longer a niche for insurers. It is a material part of the industry's balance sheet, and its performance in a slowdown will be watched by ratings agencies, regulators and investors. This article summarises published reporting and is not investment advice.
source_name: Moody's Ratings (via Insurance Business and Reinsurance News)
image_alt: US life insurers private credit liquidity concentration risk Moody's 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: Moody's says US life insurers' private and illiquid bonds reached $807 billion at year-end 2025, about 20% of a $4 trillion fixed income portfolio, up from $685 billion (18%) a year earlier.
The ten largest insurers hold $352 billion, or 44%, of those assets, although they hold only 24% of industry fixed income.
The private book is 43% NAIC 2 and 9% below investment grade, against 36% and 5% for the whole portfolio; 38% of 2025 purchases were asset-backed securities.
Payment-in-kind exposure is 1.1% of statutory surplus, which Moody's views as moderate but a possible late-cycle indicator.
Barclays found private credit holdings grew by more than 20% in 2025; Proskauer's default index rose to 2.73% in Q1 2026 from 1.84% two quarters earlier.
why_it_matters: Life insurers hold the long-term savings of millions of policyholders. If the private assets backing annuities and policies turn out harder to sell or weaker in credit quality than expected, the effect would reach customers, regulators and the wider credit market.

title: Canadian Insurers Turn to Satellite Imagery and Laser Scans to Judge Wildfire Risk Property by Property
summary: A CBC report of June 8, 2026 says insurers increasingly assess wildfire risk property by property with satellite imagery and laser scanning, rewarding FireSmart measures; one Nova Scotia owner who rebuilt saw her premium fall about 12%.
description:
How much you pay for home insurance in Canada may increasingly depend on what a satellite and a laser scanner see around your house, not on what happened in your region in the past. That is the central point of a CBC News report published on June 8, 2026, and republished by Yahoo News Canada, which describes how insurers are changing the way they judge wildfire risk. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article quoted national home-insurance inflation of 4.01% and a rise of 9.29% in Alberta premiums, and said affordability may become Canada's defining insurance crisis. The CBC report we reviewed does not contain these figures or that conclusion, and we could not verify them elsewhere, so they have been removed.

What is changing? According to the report, insurers are moving away from judging risk by a region's fire history and toward assessing individual properties. They use satellite imagery and laser scanning, known as LiDAR, to examine factors such as how close trees are to a building, the roofing and building materials used, and how well the property is maintained. In effect, two houses on the same street may be assessed differently if one has a cleared buffer zone and fire-resistant materials and the other does not.

Why not rely on past fires? The report quotes actuary Mohan Sivapatham, who explains that wildfires differ from floods in an important way. After a forest has burned, it loses the fuel for future fires, and it takes years to regrow. That means a region's past wildfire record can say little about its future risk, in either direction. A recently burned area may be less likely to burn again for a time, while an unburned area full of dry fuel may be at greater risk. He argues, in the report's words, that looking at models and model results is even more important than relying on past data. Models can combine information about vegetation, weather, terrain and buildings in ways that a historical claims record cannot.

What does this look like for a homeowner? The report gives an example. After the 2023 wildfires in Nova Scotia, Tricia Murray rebuilt her home in Hammonds Plains. Her premium then fell by about 12%. Her insurance agent credited the home's fire-resistant materials and the cleared buffer zone around it. Her subdivision, Highland Park, became the first in the Halifax region to earn an official FireSmart designation. FireSmart Canada is a programme that gives homeowners and communities guidance on reducing wildfire risk. Sivapatham says insurers are starting to factor such community measures into premiums. This is one case, and the report does not say that all homeowners would see similar reductions, so readers should not treat it as typical.

What does the Insurance Bureau of Canada say? Amanda Dean of the Insurance Bureau of Canada says these tools let homeowners lower their risk by following FireSmart Canada guidelines. That fits the logic of property-level assessment: if insurers can see what a homeowner has done, they can reward it. The report does not describe the specific discounts that any insurer offers, and they differ by company and province.

What happened in Nova Scotia? The 2023 Upper Tantallon fire caused $165 million in insured damage, destroyed 151 homes and displaced 16,000 people, according to the report. It is one of the events that has led insurers and communities in Atlantic Canada to take wildfire more seriously, a risk that was long associated with western provinces.

What are the limits of the approach? Property-level assessment relies on data and models, which can be wrong or hard for homeowners to challenge. A homeowner whose property is rated high-risk because of a satellite image may want to know what data was used and how to correct errors. The report does not discuss how insurers handle disputes, and we have not seen a published industry standard on it. Another limit is that individual action has limits: a homeowner can clear brush, but cannot control the risk of a neighbour's property or the surrounding forest. That is why community measures matter.

What can homeowners do? Practical steps suggested by the logic of the report include asking an insurer or broker what risk factors it considers, following FireSmart guidance on clearing vegetation and using non-combustible materials, and asking whether discounts are available for completing assessments or upgrades. A separate Bloomberg report, covered on this site, says Canadian insurers are encouraging owners to fortify homes and are offering some discounts for risk assessments or fire-resistant roofing and siding.

Overall, and in short, the report describes a gradual shift in how insurers price a risk that is becoming more frequent and more costly. It is based on interviews and examples, not on industry-wide data. This article is general information and is not insurance advice.
source_name: CBC News (republished by Yahoo News Canada, June 8, 2026)
image_alt: Canada wildfire risk satellite laser scanning home insurance premiums 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: Insurers are moving away from judging wildfire risk by a region's fire history and toward assessing each property, using satellite imagery and laser scanning.

The tools examine tree proximity, roofing and building materials and maintenance; the Insurance Bureau of Canada's Amanda Dean says they let homeowners lower risk by following FireSmart Canada guidelines.

After rebuilding her Hammonds Plains, Nova Scotia, home following the 2023 wildfires, Tricia Murray's premium fell about 12%, which her agent attributed to fire-resistant materials and a cleared buffer zone.
Actuary Mohan Sivapatham says a burned forest loses fuel for years, so models matter more than past data: 'Looking at models and model results is even more important than relying on past data.'
The 2023 Upper Tantallon fire caused $165 million in insured damage, destroyed 151 homes and displaced 16,000 people.
why_it_matters: As wildfire risk grows, insurers are shifting from broad area pricing to individual property assessment. That can reward homeowners who protect their houses, but it also means some owners may find that cover costs more or is harder to get.

title: Ontario's Auto Insurance Overhaul Takes Effect July 1, 2026: Only Medical, Rehabilitation and Attendant Care Stay Mandatory
summary: From July 1, 2026, most Ontario accident benefits become optional for all customers; FSRA's guidance says medical, rehabilitation and attendant care stay mandatory, existing policies renew unchanged until customers agree in writing.
description:
Ontario drivers will have more choice over their auto insurance from July 1, 2026, and more responsibility for making that choice well. The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) has published guidance for insurers on the changes, which make most statutory accident benefits optional. This article summarises that guidance and Insurance Business Canada's reporting on the debate around it. An earlier version of this article cited a source about British Columbia as its main reference. That source mentions Ontario only briefly, so this version is built on FSRA's own questions and answers for insurers. It is a summary for general information and not insurance advice; drivers should read their own renewal documents.

What changes on July 1? FSRA says the changes apply to all customers, not only to new business. Medical, rehabilitation and attendant care benefits remain mandatory. All other accident benefits become optional. The optional benefits apply only to the named insured, their spouse, dependants of either, and people listed as drivers of the insured vehicle, and FSRA encourages insurers to list all drivers. There are nine new optional coverages. FSRA's preferred practice is to offer each individually, although insurers may bundle related coverages if the bundles reflect consumer need. Customers must be able to decline higher-cost coverages regardless of bundle options, and a single bundle of all nine is not considered enough choice.

What happens to existing policies? According to FSRA, existing policies renew with the same coverages and limits until the customer agrees to a change in writing. There is no time limit on that. Renewing customers may keep their current coverage, adopt the new standard, or opt out of optional caregiver and housekeeping coverages. Customers who opt out receive the post-July 2026 offerings. For mid-term vehicle additions or substitutions, insurers must allow optionality, with the process left to the insurer provided it is transparent and fair. In practice, a driver who does nothing keeps what they have, which is meant to prevent people from losing cover by accident.

What about caregiver, housekeeping and home maintenance benefits? Before July 1, 2026, these were mandatory, with catastrophic impairment and prescribed limits as the standard and non-catastrophic cover as an optional buy-up. On or after July 1, 2026, they are optional. 'All impairments' is the legislated standard, with no prescribed limits. New business may also receive a catastrophic-only buy-down if it is filed and approved. FSRA says new business quotes must offer all impairments, and that if a quote defaults to a single option, the default must be all impairments.

What must insurers tell customers? Quotes must clearly show which coverages are optional, the premium for each, and a plain-language explanation. Customers should see all available optional coverages and limits even when one is recommended. Digital customers should be able to add or remove optional coverages without an agent, and support should be available for people who are unsure which coverages they need. FSRA stresses that communications must be clear, transparent and fair, and that they supplement, not replace, the reform information in the renewal package. Underwriting decline rules are not permitted for optional coverages, though eligibility rules for new higher limits are allowed under section 238 of the Insurance Act if they meet the Act and FSRA's fair consumer principles.

How do filings work? Insurers file their products and rates with the regulator. FSRA describes an accelerated path with a decision in 30 business days, which uses standard cost benchmarks, and a regular path for filings during the August to September window. Insurers can use their own cost assumptions instead of the Oliver Wyman study, but must explain any differences. The total premium across the optional coverages must be reasonable. There is no minimum premium benchmark for small coverages, but any increase on one must be offset by reductions elsewhere.

What is the debate? Insurance Business Canada reports that supporters say the changes give consumers choice and could reduce costs for drivers who opt out of certain protections, while critics warn that the reforms risk leaving drivers dangerously underinsured. Both views are plausible. A driver who is young, healthy and has other benefits through an employer might reasonably choose less cover, while a self-employed driver or a family with limited savings may find that an injury without income replacement or caregiver support is financially severe. The reports we reviewed do not provide estimates of premium savings, so this article does not suggest any figure.

What should drivers do? Read the renewal package carefully, compare the optional coverages and their prices, check what benefits are available through work or other policies, and ask the broker or insurer to explain any item that is unclear. Drivers who are unsure can keep their existing coverage, since policies renew unchanged until they agree in writing to a change.

This article reports regulator guidance and press coverage and does not constitute insurance, legal or financial advice.
source_name: FSRA (Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario) guidance and Insurance Business Canada
image_alt: Ontario Canada auto insurance reform accident benefits optional 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: Changes take effect July 1, 2026 and apply to all customers, not only new business; medical, rehabilitation and attendant care benefits stay mandatory and other accident benefits become optional.
There are nine new optional coverages; customers must be able to decline higher-cost coverages even where bundles are offered.
Existing policies renew with the same coverages and limits until the customer agrees to a change in writing, with no time limit.
Caregiver, housekeeping and home maintenance cover becomes optional, with 'all impairments' as the legislated standard for new business.
Insurers must show which coverages are optional, each coverage's premium and a plain-language explanation, and digital customers should be able to add or remove coverages without an agent.
why_it_matters: Ontario is Canada's largest auto insurance market. The reform could lower premiums for drivers who choose less cover, but critics warn that people who opt out of benefits may be left underinsured after a serious crash.

title: Singapore's New Integrated Shield Plan Rider Rules: A 5% Co-Payment Capped at S$6,000 and Premiums About 30% Lower
summary: From April 1, 2026, new Integrated Shield Plan riders in Singapore must include a 5% co-payment capped at S$6,000 a year and exclude the minimum deductible, a design the Ministry of Health says is about 30% cheaper than maximum-coverage riders.
description:
Singapore has changed the design of the optional riders that sit on top of Integrated Shield Plans, the private health insurance most residents use to upgrade the national MediShield Life scheme. The Ministry of Health (MOH) set out the framework in a parliamentary answer published on its website, with the new design taking effect on April 1, 2026. This article summarises what MOH says. An earlier version of this article also reported a medical inflation figure of 16.9%, an 84% premium cut by one insurer and a new MediSave rule for fertility preservation. MOH's own page on fertility preservation describes only the existing rule, which allows MediSave withdrawals up to a lifetime limit of S$15,000 per patient for treatments including egg freezing for medical reasons, and it does not confirm a June 2026 expansion, so those statements have been removed.

Some background helps. MediShield Life is the basic national health insurance scheme. Integrated Shield Plans (IPs) are private plans that add cover for private hospitals or higher ward classes. A rider is an optional add-on to an IP that pays some or all of the costs the IP leaves to the patient, namely the deductible, which is a fixed amount paid first, and the co-insurance, a percentage of the remaining bill. A rider that covers everything leaves the patient with almost nothing to pay, which makes the cost of treatment less visible and, as the minister put it, encourages over-servicing and over-consumption.

The new rules do three main things. First, the new riders include a co-payment of 5% of the bill, capped at S$6,000 a year, in addition to the deductible. Second, the new riders will not cover the minimum IP deductible, a fixed sum that the patient pays. Third, the rules apply to riders bought on or after November 27, 2025. Existing riders are not covered by the new requirements, and insurers decide how to handle them. The riders continue to protect against very large and unexpected bills, since the cap on the co-payment limits what a patient pays in a bad year.

MOH explains the change using cost data. The minister said premiums for IP riders for private hospitals grew by an average of 17% a year over the past three years, about double the growth of IP premiums themselves and faster than MediShield Life premiums. About 100,000 policyholders cancel or downgrade their riders each year, which suggests that cost is becoming a burden. The ministry said new riders are on average about 30% cheaper than existing maximum-coverage riders. As an example, a 60-year-old on maximum coverage could save about S$1,600 a year in premiums, or S$4,800 over three years, which the minister said would offset the higher co-payment for a typical procedure such as a S$3,300 knee replacement in a private hospital. These figures apply only to private hospital patients.

What will patients actually pay? MediSave, the national medical savings account, can be used to pay much of the co-payment. The minister projected that six in ten claimants would pay no cash out of pocket after using MediSave. Of the remaining four in ten, most with cash out-of-pocket would pay S$1,000 or less, and nearly all would pay S$3,000 or less. For a patient with a very large bill, the 5% co-payment is limited by the S$6,000 annual cap, and this is where the rider continues to provide protection.

The ministry also gave a second reason that is about the health system and not only cost. The share of patients treated in private hospitals fell from 15% in 2010 to 12% in 2020 and is now about 10%. The minister noted that some patients prefer public hospitals because of their range of specialties and holistic care. MOH will monitor the impact, especially in the short term, since some patients may switch to public hospitals to avoid the co-payment. It said it is expanding hospital beds and outpatient capacity and may introduce surge capacity for selected treatments. The page does not give targets or timelines for that capacity.

There are open questions that the parliamentary answer does not settle. It does not say whether insurers will allow policyholders to keep older, higher-coverage riders, or how older policyholders will be protected from reductions in cover. Those issues were raised in Parliament, but the answers recorded on the page do not address them directly. Readers who already hold a rider should check with their insurer or adviser what will happen to their policy at renewal, and whether switching would mean accepting the new co-payment.

Regulation is shared. MOH and the Monetary Authority of Singapore both oversee IP insurers. MOH sets key parameters such as co-payment and deductible rules and says it intervenes only when serious market failure appears. It consults insurers, providers and consumer representatives through the Multilateral Healthcare Insurance Committee.

For consumers, the practical message is to compare the lower premium with the higher out-of-pocket exposure, keeping in mind how much MediSave they have available to pay co-payments. For insurers, the reform is intended to slow claims growth and keep riders sustainable. For other markets facing rising health premiums, Singapore's approach, which keeps broad protection but restores some cost sharing, is an example to watch. MOH's page gives the policy intent and projections, and the real test will be claims data and premium changes in the years after April 2026.
image_alt: Singapore healthcare insurance MediSave Integrated Shield Plan reform 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: The new rider design takes effect on April 1, 2026 and applies to riders bought on or after November 27, 2025; insurers decide how to treat riders bought earlier.
New riders must include a co-payment of 5% of the bill, capped at S$6,000 a year, and will not cover the minimum Integrated Shield Plan deductible.
MOH says new riders are on average about 30% cheaper than existing maximum-coverage riders; a 60-year-old on maximum cover could save about S$1,600 a year.
Rider premiums for private hospitals grew an average of 17% a year over the past three years, about double the growth of Integrated Shield Plan premiums.
The minister projects six in ten claimants would pay no cash out-of-pocket after MediSave, and nearly all of the rest would pay S$3,000 or less.
why_it_matters: Riders that cover almost every dollar of a bill can encourage more treatment and push premiums up for everyone. Singapore is trading some cost-sharing for cheaper premiums, a choice that other markets with rising health insurance costs are watching.

title: KBRA Argues for a 'More Balanced' View of the NAIC's Private Letter Rating Review, Saying Capital Impact Is Not the Same as Credit Loss
summary: KBRA's June 8, 2026 research says private letter ratings are not synonymous with private credit and that a higher regulatory capital charge differs from a realised loss; the NAIC amendment's January 2026 start has been delayed.
description:
A credit rating agency has asked for calm in a debate about how US insurance regulators should treat privately rated bonds. On June 8, 2026, KBRA published research titled "Private Credit: A More Balanced Review of the NAIC PLR Review Process for Insurance Balance Sheets." The research responds to concern about the National Association of Insurance Commissioners' power to challenge credit ratings on private assets held by life insurers. This article summarises KBRA's release and adds background from earlier coverage. An earlier version of this article attributed the NAIC's challenge power to a threshold of notches and discussed the amendment as already operating. KBRA's release says the original January 2026 implementation has been delayed, so the article now reflects that. Because KBRA is a rating agency that issues private ratings, its views should be read as those of an interested party.

What is the background? According to KBRA, in August 2024 the NAIC adopted an amendment, called the Discretion Amendment, that lets its Securities Valuation Office (SVO) review and challenge credit ratings it does not consider a reasonable measure of risk for regulatory purposes. The amendment has focused attention on private letter ratings, or PLRs: ratings that a rating agency provides to an investor or issuer privately, without publishing them. They matter because insurers often use them to determine regulatory capital requirements. If the SVO decides that a rating is too generous, the insurer may have to hold more capital against the bond.

Why has this become controversial? Earlier reporting by FI Desk described a 2024 paper from the NAIC's Capital Markets Bureau, later withdrawn by the NAIC, which found that in 2023 nearly all of the 109 securities that moved to PLRs received higher ratings than the SVO assigned, by an average of 2.74 notches. The paper reported that smaller rating providers averaged a 3.01-notch gap, against 1.9 for larger ones. FI Desk also reported that PLR use by US insurers rose 86% between 2019 and 2023. The withdrawal of the paper, and the argument between rating agencies that followed, show how contested the evidence is. KBRA's release does not repeat these figures. It makes a different argument.

What does KBRA argue? First, PLRs are not the same as private credit. They span a range of asset types and transaction structures, so the effect of an SVO review on capital depends on the particular security, its structure, collateral, rating level and NAIC designation. Second, the capital effects are likely to be security-specific, depending on the size, rating category, NAIC designation and insurer-level concentration of affected holdings. Third, sensitivity of risk-based capital (RBC) is not the same as economic loss. KBRA explains that higher statutory bond charges can increase authorised control level RBC and lower the RBC ratio if total adjusted capital is unchanged, but that this is not a realised credit loss, an impairment or a reduction in statutory surplus. Fourth, an insurer's financial strength depends on more than statutory RBC metrics. KBRA cites asset-liability management, investment governance, earnings capacity, reinsurance, enterprise capital resources and potential management actions.

What does KBRA say about its own ratings? The agency says it applies the same methodologies, rating scales and committee processes to published and unpublished ratings. The only difference, it says, is distribution: public ratings appear on KBRA's website, while private ratings go to the engaging entity through a virtual data room. It points to its annual Global Rating Stability and Transition Study, covering 2011 to 2025 and including both published and private ratings, as indicating stability, and to a separate study, "Private Credit SF: How KBRA Ratings Stack Up," as reporting consistent performance for both types. The release contains no figures on RBC, capital or the market, and it does not name its author. Readers cannot verify KBRA's performance claims from the release alone.

How does this fit with other analysis? Moody's, in a report covered elsewhere on this site, says US life insurers' private and illiquid bonds reached $807 billion at the end of 2025, and that 91% carry an investment-grade-equivalent designation. Moody's also warns that impairment rates in private credit could exceed those of liquid holdings in a downside scenario. KBRA and Moody's are therefore not in direct conflict: one argues that the regulatory process should be judged carefully, while the other flags risks in the assets. Both agree that the details matter.

What should readers take from this? The debate is about method and evidence, and the final design of the NAIC process has not been completed in the sources reviewed. A higher capital charge on a bond reduces an insurer's flexibility, but it does not by itself mean that the bond will default. Conversely, a capital rule that is too lenient could allow insurers to hold less capital than their risks justify. Policyholders cannot judge this alone; they can look at an insurer's financial strength ratings from several agencies and at its disclosures. This article reports a published research release and is not investment advice.
image_alt: KBRA private letter ratings NAIC life insurer private credit analysis 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: KBRA says the NAIC's 'Discretion Amendment', adopted in August 2024, lets the Securities Valuation Office challenge credit ratings it does not consider a reasonable measure of risk; its original January 2026 implementation has been delayed.
KBRA stresses that private letter ratings (PLRs) are not synonymous with private credit, so the capital effect depends on the specific security, structure, collateral, rating and NAIC designation.
Higher statutory bond charges can raise authorised control level RBC and lower the RBC ratio, but that is not a realised credit loss, impairment or fall in statutory surplus.
KBRA says it applies the same methodologies and committee processes to published and private ratings, and cites its rating stability studies as showing consistent performance.
KBRA is itself a rating agency, so its view is an interested one; earlier NAIC-related analysis found large gaps between some PLRs and the SVO's own ratings.
why_it_matters: Insurers hold huge bond portfolios, and capital rules decide how much they must set aside. How regulators treat privately rated assets affects insurer capital, the supply of private credit and, ultimately, the cost and security of annuities and life insurance.
